1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
13	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
14	- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
15	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
16	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
17	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
18	
19	## How to commit
20	
21	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
22	
23	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
24	
25	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
26	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
27	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
28	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
29	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
30	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
31	
32	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
33	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
34	
35	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
36	
37	## Pushing
38	
39	Push after every commit.
40	
41	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
42	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree leaves its branch. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
43	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
44	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
45	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
46	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
47	
48	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
49	
50	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The platform rebuilds a lost container from `blinded-fable`.
51	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
52	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
53

1	# Running tests
2	
3	**track**
4	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.
5	
6	**shard**
7	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
8	
9	**code state**
10	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.
11	
12	## The two suites
13	
14	`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:
15	
16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.
20	
21	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.
22	
23	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
24	
25	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
26	
27	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
28	
29	The two suites work in the same way:
30	
31	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
32	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
33	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
34	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
35	
36	To run a suite:
37	
38	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
39	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
40	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
41	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
42	
43	## The switches that the harness reads
44	
45	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
46	
47	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
48	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
49	- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
50	- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
51	- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
52	- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.
53	
54	## Outside the gate
55	
56	- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
57	- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
58	  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
59	  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
60	  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
61	  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
62	  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
63	- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).
64	
65	## When to run a whole suite
66	
67	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
68	- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
69	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
70	  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
71	  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
72	- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
73	- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
74	- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the runtime (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
75	- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.
76	
77	The suites do not check these:
78	
79	- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
80	- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
81	- the linker's aliasing of apis;
82	- `fortress unparse`;
83	- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
84	- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.
85	
86	If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.
87	
88	## One test, or a few
89	
90	Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.
91	
92	### Interpreter tests
93	
94	Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:
95	
96	    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
97	        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
98	
99	- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
100	- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
101	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
102	- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
103	- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
104	- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
105	- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.
106	
107	To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:
108	
109	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss
110	
111	The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").
112	
113	### Compiled tests
114	
115	Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).
116	
117	The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.
118	
119	    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
120	        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1
121	
122	- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
123	- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
124	- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
125	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
126	- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
127	- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.
128	
129	To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:
130	
131	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test
132	
133	Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.
134	
135	## One unit-test class, or one track
136	
137	To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.
138	
139	To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:
140	
141	- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
142	- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
143	- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
144	- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.

1	# The specification
2	
3	Three folders hold the team's specification:
4	
5	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
6	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
7	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
8	
9	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
10	
11	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
12	
13	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
14	
15	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
16	
17	## Changing the text: the revision form
18	
19	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
20	
21	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
22	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
23	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
24	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
25	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
26	
27	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
28

# Rung T: the record

## Findings

1. **A compiled method's JVM parameters follow its declaration.** One parameter of a declared tuple type is the tuple's elements, one JVM parameter each, and the body makes the tuple again (`CodeGen.addParams`); one parameter whose declared type names a type parameter is one JVM parameter at every instance, the boxed tuple where the instance makes it a tuple, as the generic trait's interface declares it (`CodeGen.paramTypeAtInstance`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:901-924`); several parameters are one JVM parameter each. Conditions: the compiled path, at the commits named above. Evidence: `compiler_tests/TupleIndexMethodCompiled.test` passes (link, run, `PASS`) and failed on the base, 'java.lang.VerifyError … Type 'TupleIndexMethodCompiled$Arr2' (current frame, stack[0]) is not assignable to 'com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32''. What it means: a call through a generic trait's type at a tuple instance takes the tuple as one value, and a call on the object of the trait's body at the tuple type takes its elements; the code generator chooses by the declarations that the receiver's type holds (`callTakesTupleBoxed`, `CodeGen.java:7375-7407`).
2. **Two bridges join an instance's boxed tuple to a body's elements.** The code generator writes, in the class of a trait or object whose body at a tuple type shadows a generic trait's method over a type parameter, a method of the interface's boxed signature that unpacks the tuple, casts each element and calls the body virtually (`tupleElementsBridge`, `CodeGen.java:950-982`, written from `dumpOverloadedMethodChaining`, `:1537-1545`). The class loader writes, in an instantiated class, beside a method whose template's one parameter is a type parameter that the instance makes a tuple type, a method of the elements that packs them and calls it (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:119-165`), never in an interface (`:130`); it is made only where a tuple type, `LTuple⟦`, is substituted for a template parameter that was not one already (`:124-128`). Evidence: `TupleIndexMethodCompiled`'s generic cases `G[\T, nat w\]` and `Sel[\T\]`, which with the loader's earlier test ended in 'ClassFormatError: Duplicate method name "get" with signature "(…FZZ32;…FZZ32;)…FZZ32;"'. What it means: every `m[i,j]` of the one library's arrays of rank 2 and 3 has its body, the rehearsal's W15.
3. **The forwarders count JVM parameters.** The forwarder of an object's method to its mangled body, and of an inherited body, loads each JVM parameter of its own signature (`CodeGen.java:3154-3159`, `:867-870`), where before it loaded one per Fortress parameter, so a method of one pair parameter loaded self and one element. ## FACTS.md

> **A compiled method's JVM parameters follow its declaration, and two bridges join an instance's boxed tuple to a body's elements.** One parameter of a declared tuple type is the tuple's elements, one JVM parameter each; one parameter whose declared type names a type parameter is one boxed JVM parameter at every instance, a tuple among them, as the generic trait's interface declares it. The code generator writes, where a body at the tuple type shadows such a method, a method of the boxed signature that calls the body with the elements (`CodeGen.tupleElementsBridge`), and a dotted call passes the tuple boxed where the receiver's type holds only such declarations (`CodeGen.callTakesTupleBoxed`); a generic dotted method of one parameter is called with the receiver and the argument as two values. The class loader writes, in an instantiated class and never in an interface, beside a method whose template's one parameter is a type parameter that the instance makes a tuple type, a method of the elements that calls it (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:119-165`). Test: `compiler_tests/TupleIndexMethodCompiled.test`. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-tuple-parameter/REPORT.md`, "The convention as built".

## Revival change

**The change.** The team's library declared the number types as traits, each comprising native objects: `trait ZZ32 extends { ZZ64, Integral[\ZZ32\] } comprises { Int, IntLiteral }`, `trait RR64 extends Number comprises { Float, FloatLiteral, RR32, QQ }` and the like (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fss:422`, `:642`, `:700`, `:770`, `:822`), with `value object Int extends ZZ32`, `Float`, `Long`, `UnsignedLong` and `BigNum` in `FortressBuiltin` (`a874948ac:ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:54`, `:369`, `:378`, `:450`, `:528`), and walk's glue classes `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum`, `UnsignedLong` built those objects; the specification presents `ZZ` as a trait (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:229`). The tree now declares each of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` as one `value object` of the one library, as `NN32` and `RR32` already were, and walk builds its values from a glue class of the type's own name: `asif` at the type is the value itself, a typecase arm at its name takes its values, its ilk is its name (`ProjectFortress/tests/NumberTypesAreObjectsWalk.fss`), and a program's object below one is refused at load, 'Attempt to extend object type ZZ32' (`ProjectFortress/tests/NumberTypeExtendRefusedWalk.fss`). A program's own number type extends `Number`. The names `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` declare nothing: as a type they are undefined, and as a typecase arm they take every value. The reason: each trait had exactly one object below it, the reasons for the split (the literal types, the nested tower) are gone; the second names are walk's internals, which a program saw as types; and a program's object below `ZZ32` loaded under walk and then failed at its first native method, 'getInt not implemented for FOrdinaryObject' (measured: `object Mine extends ZZ32` loaded and printed `Mine` on 647163a9c4), while on the compiled path such an object compiles and dies when its class loads, 'class ...$Mine can not implement com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32, because it is not an interface', since a bare `int` cannot hold it.

6df780a7d0 The compiled code casts self where it stands at a type below its trait

Climb batch 31, rung K (rows 991 and 695). The checker reads a comprises
clause at the level of values, so in trait Q comprises { R } self may
stand where R is expected, and in a self-typed trait self may be returned
as the implementing type. The code generator emitted no cast there, and
the JVM's verifier refused the class when it loaded. It now casts a value
that has self's type to a declared type strictly below its trait, at a
single argument, a typed binding, an assignment and a method's returned
value, also where the value is a typecase whose arms are each self.
Appendix I's sentence on a default body that returns self says that it
runs. Rows 1050 to 1053 are new: a closure's returned self, a
conditional's arm, a call on a value of the self-type parameter, and an
assignment of a subtype's value to a var field from outside its object.

This commit edits the original tree.

407	### Rung M, `rung-method-forwarders`: the methods that a class inherits
408	
409	**The change.** The team's code generator (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`, `dumpMethodChaining`, with `STypesUtil.removeIdenticallyCoveredMethods`, `scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1574`) wrote a forwarder for each inherited declaration with a body that no declaration of a subtype covered, comparing the two domains as schemas over each trait's own static parameters; it skipped every declaration without a body, an imported api's among them. So a compiled generic trait that declared again a method which it inherited through a trait that was not its first could not load, and a compiled object could not call a method whose body an imported api's trait gave it, unless that trait was first in its extends clause. The tree now writes one method for each such group, which runs the declaration of the lowest type that declares it, as walk does, and forwards to the api trait's body: `compiler_tests/TraitOwnMethodBesideInheritedCompiled`, `compiler_tests/ApiTraitMethodNotFirstCompiled`. The reason: the traits chapter, section "Method Declarations" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:584-590`), by which a trait does not inherit a declaration whose parameter types are those of one that it declares; the measured failures 'ClassFormatError: Duplicate method name "mx?0"' and 'AbstractMethodError ... does not define or inherit an implementation'; and the compiled checker's reading of an api's method without `abstract` as one with a body (`scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala:274`). A programmer no longer needs to put an api's trait first in an extends clause, or to keep a generic trait from declaring again what it inherits. Two limits stay: an object's own overloads of a functional method with self not first beside an inherited one still die at dispatch, and a body of a self-typed trait that returns `self` still fails verification at an object instance.

415	### Rung L, `rung-label-exit`: label and exit on the compiled path
416	
417	#### The change
418	
419	The team's code generator had no case for a label block or an exit: `CodeGen` declared no `forLabel` and no `forExit`, so the node reached `defaultCase`, which refused the declaration with 'Can't compile Label' (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1859`, `defaultCase`). Walk runs both, and matches an exit to a label by the label's name (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:628-645`, `:500-519`); its `try` offers an exit that passes it to the `catch` clauses as the library's `LabelException` (`Evaluator.java:1453-1456`).
420	
421	The tree now compiles both (`CodeGen.java:1776-1857`, `runtimeSystem/LabelExit.java`). A compiled exit leaves the evaluation of the label block in which it was made, also from the body of a `for`, from a function expression and from another task; a parallel loop first joins the iterations that it forked, which run to their end or to their own exit; the label's value is one of the exiting values. No compiled `catch` clause takes an exit. Test: `compiler_tests/LabelExitCompiled`. Where a label block is evaluated again inside itself, a compiled exit leaves the evaluation in which its function was made, and walk's leaves the innermost one: `descend` of `compiler_tests/LabelEvaluationIdentityCompiled` gives 102 compiled and 104 under walk.
